Messages.Author: James A Ignatuk
Messages.Body:
I played a game of Jyhad the other week, and my friend managed to
grave-rob five vampires. However, when those Methuelahs were ousted,
all the graverobbed vampires suddenly left play with their owners.

This doesn't really seem right. My reasoning here is this: he
_gained_ control of them by graverobbing. Therefore, those minions
should be treated just as if he influenced them from his own crypt, and
shouldn't leave play when his prey is ousted.

I don't get this ruling of "all cards leave play when the owning
Methuselah leaves the game."

The way I see it is this: Methuselahs play cards and "bring them
into the Jyhad world." And once they're in the "Jyhad world," they're
there for the rest of the game unless burnt. It doesn't matter who
controls them, they're still in the game. And if a Methuselah is
ousted, he's just dead and that's it. It doesn't make sense that the
controlling Methuselah suddenly "forgets" that he was controlling five
vampires which he worked so hard to steal from another Methuselah...

The explaination I've heard for the ruling is this: the Methuselah
who brings a card into play somehow puts a "blood bond" on the card
which cannot be replaced. Even if a card is taken control of by another
Methuselah, the original Methuselah is still that card's "Sire" and when
that Meth. leaves the game, all his influence leaves with him, thus
explaining why cards leave the game no matter who controls them.

But this explaination is STUPID!!! That sounds more like a Magical
control than an actual control, and this is Jyhad, not Magic!!! It's
like trying to say that a vampire dies when his sire is burnt, and
that's just dumb.

If anyone has any better explainations, or if anyone agrees, or even
disagrees, please post.

Take care,
Jim

The rule is there so that players who are ousted may move on if that is
their wish. I have been ousted very early from a nine player game while
some of the other players had control of my cards. It would not haver
been fun waiting up to five hours to get them back while not playing with
that deck again. It is a rule of convenience and if I was not leaving or
knew the other players well then I would let them keep them if all agreed.

Sam

The real explanation:

VtES is a Collectible card game. The golden rule of card ownership
means that the cards you bring to play with are the cards you leave
with. When you are ousted, the cards you brought are returned to you,
so that you may leave with them.

Messages.Author: Dave Green
Messages.Body:
James A Ignatuk (igna...@andrew.cmu.edu) wrote:

: Alright, this seems to be a fair ruling... :) But do you think it'd

: be fair if the cards remained in play until the end of the game? (If,
: of course, the players all agreed to play that way...)
: I think this would make the game cooler, because the "cards leave
: with the Methusaleh" ruling really kills corruption decks, and stealing
: equipment decks, or anything which takes advantage of gaining control of
: stuff, etc...

Of course that is a fair way to play, and the one that makes
the most sense. The Golden Rule of card ownership is fine in
the tournament setting when you are likely to leave and find
something else interesting to do after being ousted, but in
your own circles, why not play the way that makes the most
sense to game mechanics. AFAIK most people do play this way.
I know that I'd be hopelessly lost in a tournament setting,
because my play group decided long ago, back when there was
only the Jyhad, that ew liked the rules and cards the way they
were, and have only changed when necessary to incorporate
genuinely new rules and concepts introduced with the
expansions. Play the way you think is best, just be prepared
to be lost at tournies if you don't come prepared.

: Take care,
: Jim

Have fun,
Dave

I was thinking about this and it seems to me that it should be the other
way round to how it is at the moment.

If I play a Setite-deck, or a Graverobbing deck, or a Chimerstry-Magpie
deck, when I oust my prey (assuming I stole my cards off them), I lose
the cards and have also wasted a lot of my deck on getting them (all the
Graverobbings, Blessing of Durga Syns and Corruptions and so on are in
my ash heap) and I probably can't get them back. thus, my deck falls
over in a heap.

Surely, once I've nicked someone's stuff, I should be able to keep it.
I've invested time and effort in Corrupting someone's vampires (perhaps
more than they did getting them out). And if a Methuselah is being
severely stamped on, it's not like they're going to have chance to see
how their <INSERT NAME OF STOLEN CARD HERE> is doing.

If you use the crappy Sabbat rules (the only good part is Camarilla
membership has its privileges and even that gets the fact that NC vamps
can't be primogens wrong - believe me, if Ravnos ask for a position on
the Primogen council, don't argue) then when you withdraw, your cards
stay in play. However, surely when you withdraw you remove all of your
influence from the Jyhad and are going to want that <INSERT NAME OF
STOLEN CARD HERE> back, for when you next participate. Presumably,
that's what you'd be doing during the turn that you have to wait whilst
your not being bled or entering combat or whatever.

So, shouldn't it be the other way round - cards leave with you when you
withdraw, but stay in play when you are ousted?

Any comments?

--

James Coupe (remove .nospam to reply)

Personally, I like to play with the cards sticking around, if the
player who owns the cards doesn't have to go anywhere. Of course, they
frequently want to start a different game, or go have lunch/dinner/breakfast
and as such will need to take the cards with them. In that case, use a proxy,
or substitute another card of the same type from another one of your decks.

However, WORK THIS OUT BEFOREHAND! Do not attempt to proxy in a card
when you have ousted your prey, because your new prey will have every right to
deny you. Changing the rules when they benefit you is cheating, changing them
before the game starts is enhancing the flavor of the game.

> Take care,
> Jim

Frank
